The house resumed from Thursday, March 10, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.

Mr. Speaker, while listening to this
debate, I have observed that hon. members on the government side are continually reiterating that no constructive suggestions have been offered by this side of the house with respect to providing for unemployment relief. Let me remind the house, and particularly hon. members opposite, that several constructive suggestions have been put forward on this side. I can recall at the moment that my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) on different occasions has suggested to the government the advisability of bringing in a supply bill providing for whatever amount they might deem necessary for the immediate continuance of unemployment relief, stating that he would guarantee, so far as the opposition was concerned, to put it through in the 
shortest possible time. On this occasion I want to repeat that offer. I would ask the government in all sincerity to bring down a supply bill this afternoon for any amount they might consider necessary to provide for the relief of unemployment, and this side will guarantee to put it through within an hour. While they are considering that suggestion, and in the hope that they will accept it, we might discuss another constructive suggestion-and again I offer this to the government in all sincerity. I suggest that at this session they might bring down a bill to provide for unemployment insurance. There is no question that an unemployment insurance system for Canada can be instituted and worked out to the best interests of the country.
Canada has been described by some people as an eight-months' country; that is to say, a great proportion of the workers of the country are employed only eight months of the year. Any of us who have observed the affairs of this dominion as they relate to labour know that there are many men who are out of work in Canada four months in every year by reason of seasonal occupations. We could, therefore, establish an unemployment insurance scheme at the outset on the basis of sixteen weeks.
As is well known, Great Britain embarked on an unemployment insurance scheme in 1911, and since that time Italy, Australia, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Poland and Germany have established compulsory insurance systems, while many other European countries have provided relief through other measures. One measure is to provide such relief by subsidizing trade union benefits. Within the British Empire itself the Irish Free State, New Zealand, and one state in Australia, namely, Queensland, have state unemployment insurance. There is little doubt about it that public opinion is now ripe for such a scheme in Canada. This House of Commons has endorsed the principle of a system of contributory unemployment insurance. The provinces were canvassed by the late Liberal government and many of them put themselves on record as in favour of the establishment of an unemployment insurance scheme. They now realize that unemployment insurance is one means of meeting the problem for those who are willing and able to work but who are unable to find employment.
Personally I have given considerable thought and study to the question of unemployment insurance as it is carried out in other countries and as it would operate in Canada. There are also several good articles on the subject, one in particular which I have

Unemployment Continuance Act
in mind having been written by Professor Harry Cassidy, director of research on the unemployment research committee of Ontario.
I refer to Professor Cassidy of Toronto university. The Prime Minister has said that he is waiting for some information. Well, we have the information that can be secured through the Dominion Bureau index, which gives the number of unemployed persons in Canada; and we have the figures collected by the Labour department showing the number of those employed in industry through trade unions, as well as the figures which we have secured through the recent census. We can therefore fairly estimate that there are about two million wage earners and low-salaried men in Canada, the percentage of unemployed being about eight per cent. If we adopted regulations precluding those who would not be entitled to benefits it would reduce the percentage to about seven. So that if we take the bulk of two millions and estimate that seven per cent are usually unemployed for at least four months in every year, there would be entitled to benefits from the fund about
140,000	persons. Assuming that the benefit range would be from $30 per month for single men and $65 for married persons, that would be $80,000,000 a year. Allowing $10,000,000 for administration expenses the total amount required to provide benefits and for administration would be $90,000,000. Assuming there would be three groups making contributions to this fund, the workers, the employers and the state. In order to raise the contribution to be made by the workers, each man would be required to contribute $15 per year or 30 cents per week; one or two per cent of the payroll of the average employer would raise the $30,000,000 required from that group and the remaining $30,000,000, would be contributed by the federal government or, if it desires to cooperate with the provinces, it could contribute $15,000,000 and the provinces the remaining $15,000,000. Such a scheme could be inaugurated and put into effect in Canada without any further delay.
There will be times when the benefits will be drawn from the fund for a longer period than four months, but this could be guarded against by a well thought out plan of public works. We must admit that cycles of unemployment and periods of depression will occur again. There has not been one ten-year period during the last sixty or eighty years which has not included a period of depression. With the intensive competition which this country is facing, with the progress wc are making in replacing man-power with machinery, with the restriction which is going
on in our world markets, we must face the situation that each recurring period of depression will be greater in extent.
In order to protect this fund from overwithdrawals during a period of depression we should change our method of conducting our public works program. I know it would be very hard for the government to restrain the members of parliament who ask for public buildings, new docks and wharves, additional dredging and other kinds of public works, but if we are to face this problem in a manful way and realize what is before us we should refrain from carrying on public works when times are good so that in times of depression we will be prepared to launch an extensive program.
The scheme must be national in scope. If only a few provinces put it into effect, there would be a run on them by the unemployed workers. Even though all the provinces put the scheme into effect at once, it would not work successfully because of the fact that so many workers in Canada travel from one province to another. There should be some central authority to direct the workers to where they are most needed. There should be no further worry with regard to our jurisdiction in the matter. Some of the provinces already have signified their willingness to cooperate in such a scheme. We have invaded the provincial field in other matters such as highway construction, technical education, employment offices and old age pensions. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has said that this government can vote money for anything which in its judgment is desirable. I do not overlook the fact that the Conservative party, now the government, received from the electors at the last elections a mandate to deal with unemployment on a national scale, and it has asked from parliament the right to do anything under any circumstances that it wishes. There is no excuse to delay any longer. Any question of waiting for further information, of gathering additional statistics or of hearing the opinions of actuaries is, to my way of thinking, only stalling off the proposition. This scheme has been tried in other countries and we have had an opportunity of observing the failures and successes of these countries and, benefiting by that knowledge, we should be able to enact a measure to provide an unemployment insurance scheme for this country. This is one more constructive suggestion which I offer to the government of the day.
I assure the government that if it will enter sincerely into this project and bring down a measure, so far as I am concerned-I know

Unemployment Continuance Act
many other hon. members on this side will do likewise-I will cooperate with the government in an effort to see that the necessary legislation is enacted during this session.
Speaking in connection with the measure before us, if it can be called a measure, I must say that it is to be regretted that the government has not presented to this house some concrete proposal to deal with the unemployment situation in Canada. With all the experience it has had and with all the criticism that has been levelled against it, one would have thought that the government would have had something better to offer than this haphazard and hit-and-miss method of dealing with unemployment. I shall not deal at this time with the many promises made to the electors during the recent elections any more than to say that the government has failed signally either to end unemployment or to provide proper methods of relief. When the supporters of the government go through the country and tell of the millions of dollars they have spent and of the work given to thousands of people, they do not deceive anyone but themselves.
The methods adopted by this government to relieve unemployment have proved utterly inadequate. We have been advised by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) that since the commencement of this undertaking, under the Unemployment Relief Act, and up to January 31 of the present year, 327,590 persons were given 7,228,744 days' work, or an average of about twenty-two days' work each in that period, and in the latter period, to take the minister's own figures, 334,301 persons were given 7,415,973 days' work or an average of twenty-two days' work each. I do not need to point out to the minister that we now have before us the report of the director of unemployment relief and the minister's figures do not exactly jibe with those contained in the report. There is, however, a difference of only about half a million days' work and 5,000 persons, but that does not alter the argument to any great extent. Therefore we have given these men an average of three days' work each per month, if you figure it from the time they first began, to the 31st January, 1932. In all sincerity I ask whether the members of the government consider that is taking care of the unemployed of Canada.
What has this cost the country? To meet this, the federal, provincial and municipal authorities have been committed to an expenditure of $146,899,219, the federal government's share being, in round figures, about $50,000,000, and that of the provincial governments and municipalities about $100,000,000.

This scheme was supposed to be launched for the purpose of giving work and wages to our unemployed. Let us see what amount out of this $146,000,000 has been paid to the workers. We find that since the beginning of the unemployment relief, if we take both periods combined, 14,644,717 days' work was supplied. At eight hours a day and at thirty cents an hour, that would amount to $2.40 a day, so that the total amount paid would be $35,147,320.80. Therefore, those who received employment did not receive even one-quarter of the total amount expended, approximately $112,000,000 having gone for some other purpose. The government has not as yet given the house any information with respect to that, but I am satisfied that at least $112,000,000 has not gone into wages for those men.
If we divide the amount paid in wages by the number of men who have been paid, we find that for sixteen months these men have received an average of $53 each. I ask members of the government or any of their supporters how they think those men can live for sixteen months on $53, and in that I am giving the government the advantage in the figures. It is not sufficient for the workers of the country, nor is it good business for the country itself. Yet we find members of the government and many of its supporters taking great credit throughout Canada for the magnificent manner in which they have contributed to the assistance of the provinces. I think in all fairness they ought to point out that while the government are pretending to contribute with the one hand to assist the provinces, they are with the other withholding from the provinces large federal expenditures and obligations.
If we take the Public Works estimates of last year and this, we shall find that last year's estimates show a reduction of $17,000,000 as compared with the previous year. That $17,000,000 would have provided a considerable amount of work from the federal government at fair rates of wages. This year's Public Works estimates show a further reduction of
810,000,000, so that in the two seasons combined, the federal government has withheld work to the extent of $27,000,000. That is not all. It will be recalled that during the recent election the Conservative party obligated themselves to take over the full cost of old age pensions. It was estimated by a committee of this house that an old age pension scheme for Canada would cost in the neighbourhood of $24,000,000. This year the government will pay not over $7,000,000, so that they are withholding $17,000,000 that

Unemployment Continuance Act
they obligated themselves to take over and pay to the provinces in connection with old age pensions. A number of the provinces have been depending upon the federal government assuming the entire cost, and several of them, relying upon the promises of the Prime Minister, have spent money in other ways.
I need not dwell upon the fact that last session there was put through the house a technical education bill, whereby the government promised the provinces a considerable amount of money which they have not received, but which, according to law, is due to them. I need not point out that the government during the last election promised to construct a national highway, the work to be carried on as a federal scheme. What is the situation? The fact is that the government has contributed 50 per cent of the expense in connection with the trans-Canada highway, requiring the provinces to pay the other half, and I think, up to the present time, according to the report, it owes the provinces somewhere in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000 which it should have paid in connection with that highway. What I want to point out is this: hon. members opposite are telling the people that the government is spending $140,000,000, when the fact is that two-thirds of that amount has been spent by the provinces instead of by the federal government. My hon. friends ought also to tell the people of the millions of dollars being withheld from the provinces because the government is not carrying out its obligations. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that from now on we do not intend to allow that kind of bluff or make-believe to go in this country.
Complaints have been made from the government side of the house that no constructive suggestion has emanated from this side. I would remind hon. members that when the right hon. the Prime Minister was leader of the opposition he declared over and over again that the government must be responsible for any measures that were brought down, and particularly he emphasized that he did not intend to prescribe until he was called in. Well, he has been called in and he has been working at his job, but up to the present time his policy has been an utter failure so far as providing work for the unemployed in this country is concerned. Further, I would say with regard to constructive suggestions, that both last session and again this session I listened to the right hon. leader of the Liberal party state in this house that if his government had been returned to power he would have dealt with the unemployment situation in a more scientific way. He would
have called in representatives of all those interested in the unemployment situation in Canada, the representatives of the provinces, of industry, commerce, labour and other interests, and surely out of such a conference there would have come, and could come yet if the government would only accept the suggestion, a far better and more equitable and more adequate policy than we have at the present time. So I hope, Mr. Speaker, that even yet the government will take that suggestion into consideration and call a conference of all those interested so that we may tackle this unemployment insurance question in a more scientific and more equitable way, and provide a more adequate system for taking care of the unemployed citizens of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate on the government's resolution which endeavours to secure discretionary powers in order to draw funds from the treasury to relieve the unemployed, farmers and those who are suffering in this crisis which is worldwide and in which Canada has not been spared. I shall refer to the causes of the present situation in order to justify my opposition to this resolution. Experience has taught us that this act has had ruinous and inefficient results, and furthermore, this bill is ultra vires at its very face.
In July, 1930, the people of Canada were called to the polls to elect a government. The Liberal party retiring after four years of administration, four years of prosperity, but at the outset of the present world-wide crisis, was seeking from the people a renewal of their mandate. Realizing the difficult situation and the problems which the incoming government would have to face, the Liberal party moved for a commission to study the question of unemployment, in order to solve this crisis, find work for the unemployed and relieve those who were in distress.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), then leader of the opposition, and his followers, travelled throughout the country advocating a different policy and being very lavish with their pledges, charging the outgoing government of being responsible for the depression existing then. Thereby they undertook to find a remedy to the crisis and bring back prosperity to this country. They stated that the Liberal government was responsible for this unemployment because of its majority in parliament by which it enacted all measures necessary for the welfare of the country. The leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister made very definite pledges as well as did hon. members on your right,
10: >2

sir, who now form the government, and on the faith of these specific pledges or promises, the people confided in the Conservative party so as to afford them an opportunity to fulfil these pledges.
What has the government done since then? What has happened since that date? Hardly more than a month after the election a special session is called so as to fulfil part of these promises and find work for the unemployed, for all who wished to work to make a living and for the farmers who were to leave their fields to seek elsewhere food for their family. Refusing to listen to the suggestion of the opposition to appoint a commission on unemployment, composed of experts in finance, industry, trade, agriculture and representatives of labour, in order to study the problem and take the necessary measures to meet the crisis which had spread over the country, the government purely and simply had $20,000,000 voted.

That is an
old story.

It cannot too often be told.
The government had $20,000,000 voted though not assuming alone the responsibility of the distribution of this fund, but they made the provinces and municipalities partly bear this responsibility and forced them to contribute and share the burden which the Conservative party had assumed at election time.
In September, 1930, when a special session was called to deal with unemployment, there were but 117,000 people without work in this country,-according to the Labour Gazette and the Dominion government statistics. Stress, must be, sir, laid on these figures. It was to relieve these 117,000 unemployed that $20,000,000 were voted, to which amount must be added $50,000,000 contributed jointly by the provinces and municipalities in a ratio which had been fixed according to circumstances which might develop, this meant an outlay of $70,000,000 to relieve the situation. Thus, $70,000,000 were expended in 1930-1931. With what result? With the disastrous result that on January 1, 1931, 62,500 people were added to the list of unemployed. The situation far from being relieved in the autumn of 1931, the number had increased to 350,000;
233,000	having been added to the September 1930 list, while millions of dollars were voted to relieve the unemployed. I trust that these gentlemen will take good note of these telling figures. The Prime Minister, in the course of the electoral campaign proclaimed through-

out the country, on every public husting and by means of radio broadcasts, that should he be raised to power, he would take the necessary measures to find work for every one who desired to work, thus putting an end to unemployment. What faith can we repose today in his new pledges?
As a proof of my contention that this policy to relieve the unemployed was a failure, I shall quote a short news item which appeared in La Patrie on September 5, 1931, dated Ottawa, and published by the Canadian Press:
The number of unemployed in Canada has increased to over 530,000, according to Mr. G. Robertson, Minister of Labour.
I think I have sufficiently established that the government's policy to relieve unemployment was a complete failure. Furthermore, to this failure must be added this exaggerated high tariff on over 200 items in connection with imports which inevitably resulted in reducing our foreign trade and the number of workmen in our factories. Owing to overproduction the manufacturers were unable to find markets for their products, while in previous years under a moderate tariff the Canadian manufacturers were able to sell abroad a great quantity of their goods, which necessarily gave work to a great number of people and provided a living for all. I shall refer later to this tariff question.
At the last session, in 1931, just before prorogation, after five months of deliberation, the government, by its majority, notwithstanding the protests of the opposition, forced through the house Bill No. 58, granting a blank cheque on the treasury, without furnishing details as provided by the statutes, and this, still with the intention of helping the unemployed, those in distress, the farmers in the west, and, to also maintain peace and good order.
What policy was followed by the government in 1931, in the expenditure of these millions of dollars in pursuance of its authority to sign a blank cheque? The government spent enormous sums, obliging the provincial governments and municipalities to contribute to these funds, hence affecting their credit, encumbering the budgets of the latter, forcing the country into debts by contracting heavy obligations, so that, to-day, the government finds it necessary to increase the ratepayers' taxes. What was the outcome of this policy? Statistics published in 1932, show us that since September, 1930, according to the figures quoted just now by the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), 334,000 unemployed were given work; representing 7,400,000 days

Unemployment Continuance Act
of work, this amounts approximately to 22 days of work for each person, at a cost of $70,500,000, or about $10 per working day, during a period of six months. Is this satisfactory? No, if we consider that the unemployment problem has not been solved and that the purpose aimed at has not been achieved, since statistics prove that the number of unemployed is larger to-day than it was in September, 1930. The Labour Gazette in its issue of January, 1932, at page 69, states that the labour market has been quieter in factories, during 1931, than in other years since 1926. The following figures are quoted: 4,400 factories, in 1930, employed 525,000 workmen; in 1931, 4,670 factories employed only 467.711 people. This is the result of the failure of the exaggerated tariff policy of this government.
Let us now examine the assistance given to farmers in the west, for whose relief millions of dollars were voted. I do not intend to criticize this measure since the government has thought fit to have such enormous sums voted; it is quite evident that the government overlooked the poor farmers of the other provinces who are in distress. I think that the other provinces should have been consulted previous to the government pledging its credit for so many millions of dollars in order to assist part of the country only. It was a matter which affected the people's money as a whole, hence this procedure cannot be approved.
The resolution begs leave to introduce a bill to extend for two months the powers by which the government was given the famous blank cheque, thus allowing it to make the same outlays as in the past. This measure is contrary to the principle of our constitution and deprives parliament of its prerogative. It is our duty, as members, to oppose this unconstitutional measure which has no precedent in our parliamentary history. When this bill asking for a blank cheque was introduced, the government first stipulated that it would end with the fiscal year; it was, however, decided later to extend it to March 1, 1932, seeing that the session was to really begin this year one or two months before March 1. This afforded an opportunity to the government to introduce this bill at an earlier date than it did. Parliament has now been sitting since February 4. Has the right hon. Prime Minister not had sufficient time to introduce heretofore this measure to solve the unemployment problem and evolve means to meet the present crisis, instead of asking parliament to extend an act which has expired and by which no solution to the unemployment question was found?

Will the
hon. member allow me to put a question? Did your constituency request you to oppose this measure?

Everybody
is discontented.

My answer
to the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) is that I was given a mandate as the hon. member was, and when I express such a view, I am certain of receiving the approval of my constituents. Anyhow, I take the whole responsibility.
The Prime Minister stated in Victoria B. C. during the election in July:
I shall call a session to give work and not dole.
I think, sir, that the Prime Minister must regret, to-day, his last words "and not dole" because he would probably have recourse to dole instead of work, especially after the experience of the outlay made in 1930 and 1931. To corroborate my statement, I shall quote figures which speak for themselves and over which, I hope, hon. members on the government side will ponder. According to the statistics relating to the work carried out in 1930-1931, to relieve unemployment, as agreed with the provinces, municipalities and railway companies, work was given to 334,000 persons, that is 7,400,000 days of work in round figures, this meant an expenditure of $70,570,000, of which $14,342,962 was provided by the Dominion government. During the same period 438,777 persons, either single or family supporters, received, I shall not say as dole, but as direct aid an amount of $7,000,000. We must bear this in mind.

Not too
much.

It is not
any too much; as we shall see. These amounts included the contributions of the provinces and municipalities. Every unemployed to whom work was given therefore cost the country $210, while in the other case, direct assistance, the cost to the country for every person relieved was $16.

Was
Taschereau opposed to this?

I am not
called upon to discuss here provincial politics. When the opportunity comes, I shall invite the hon. member to discuss them.

We shall
be there.

Any one,
sir, who wishes to give himself the trouble can easily compare these figures and prove to his satisfaction that the assistance given through work cost the treasury fourteen times more than direct aid, for each person relieved.

Be
serious.

I am absolutely so and I challenge the hon. member to deny these figures. Then, why not have brought down a measure substituting direct assistance instead of assistance through work, since we have to deal with an expenditure of millions of dollars, of enormous sums drawn from the treasury.

What do
you suggest?

I have just
mentioned it. If the hon. member did not catch my words, I would beg of him to listen more closely to my remarks. He will have an opportunity to read Hansard and he will then understand what I said.

Cross over,
you will hear better.

May I request the hon. member to have the courage to rise and deliver a speech in his turn.
The country, sir, would be $55,000,000 less in debt, if the government had adopted the system of direct assistance to the unemployed. Are you aware how much the government would have economized? $5,000,000, per year, in interest on the amounts expended on unemployment. These figures are worthy of consideration and constitute a sufficient motive to oppose the present resolution.
Where do these figures come from?

From statistics. I think I have sufficiently shown the grounds on which I base my views on this question. I shall close my remarks by asking that we all cooperate and have confidence, while we are passing through this difficult period. It is most encouraging to note that notwithstanding the critical stages through which all nations passed during this crisis, nothing happened to affect Canada's resources and dampen its faith in the future. Her lands, forests, mines, water powers and farms constitute an asset which is an assurance for the future and a stimulus to further effort. The skill shown by Canadians to utilize their resources has in no way diminished. In times of depression and distress, when the economic

equilibrium is upset, it is a national duty to introduce measures to meet the existing conditions. A true appreciation of our national resources and the wealth which industry and labour can produce give rise to real confidence in the future, and this confidence must be the foundation of all improvement in our economic conditions. However, it behooves Parliament to pass laws which have no connection with radical measures, pull down tariff walls, substitute a moderate tariff and foreign trade treaties which will re-establish throughout the world the trade relations which were so advantageous to Canada during the last period, and which I think, is the only solution possible to the unemployment problem in Canada as well as abroad.

I had not intended to take part in this debate as I wished to allow members of the legal profession the task of pondering over the constitutional aspect of the resolution under discussion. I had hoped that the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) would give us the benefit of his professional training but I fear that it will be denied to us. We should, however, rejoice in having been enlightened by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion) who perhaps does not shine as brightly as the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Duranleau). At the risk of appearing discourteous towards the former, I shall state that his legal attainments seem rather dull compared with those of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). I shall ask him to follow the advice which he ventured to give to the hon. member for Quebec East and further suggest that he send a copy of his speech to the Prime Minister of Quebec, who will not need a great effort of mind to perceive the difference between the two speeches.
The hon. member for Quebee-Montmorency was entirely outside of the subject discussed and alluded to a certain measure adopted by the Quebec legislature and which, I think, did not please our Conservative friends of that province: the famous Dillon Act.
It is certainly famous.

I shall say to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency that this legislation was enacted to redeem the honour of the province of Quebec, attacked and outraged by a mountebank using the election funds, the source of which is as well known by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency as that of Beauharnois. The hon. member has no right to insinuate that the

Liberals of Quebec stole the election in the last provincial campaign. His charge is absolutely false and untrue. He has neither the right to insult the people of Quebec by insinuating that they were bought.
Mr. DORIOiN (Translation): They were robbed, it is quite a different story.
The hon. member has no right to insult his fellow citizens of Quebec.	.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency contends that the hon. member for St. Denis is reading his speech.
Mr. DENIS '(Translation): No, I have simply some notes.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): You are not consistent.

It is preferable to what you do, as you never read.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): It is better not to open one's mouth than to say stupidities.

It is redeeming the honour of Quebec to pass an act in protest against such an outrage to the respectability of the citizens of that province.
I shall be brief, sir, in my remarks to the house in connection with the resolution under discussion. I do not intend to take more than a few minutes discussing this question, but I believe that the people whom I represent in this house will expect me, on a resolution of such importance, affecting as it does the very foundations of our governmental institutions, to express my views. In a recent debate in this house some of us, including myself, were accused of not giving full credit to the government for what they have done in the way of meeting the unemployment situation during the past year. We are prepared to give the government full credit for all they have done, and we realize that they have had a gigantic task on their hands. That, however, does not prevent us from voicing criticism when we realize that mistakes have been made.
I am fully aware of the conditions that exist in the province of Saskatchewan. Last summer I had an opportunity of driving through about 150 miles of territory where not a spear of anything was to be seen growing, except Russian thistles, and in all that territory the only machines I saw employed were two machines which were cutting Russian thistle. The conditions were terrible and it was necessary for the government to do a good deal towards relieving the situation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), told us a few days ago that 300,000 people had been given relief in Saskatchewan. That, I believe, is true and we give the government credit for what they have done in this regard. The thing we object to is this, that in the session of 1930, there was enacted such legislation as rendered this relief necessary to the extent to which it was given. Let me explain what I mean. Had we a market in Saskatchewan for our beef, pork, mutton, wool, butter, eggs, poultry and such other produce as we have on our farms, this unemployment relief would have been in large measure unnecessary. Our British preference in 1930 was wiped out. We have practically no market for anything we have to sell, and outside of a few municipalities, where there was absolutely nothing, around the borders of that area in the proving of Saskatchewan there was plenty of feed available, so that if the farmers had a propel market they would not have found it necessary, at least to the extent they did, to look for assistance.
Probably the Prime Minister is not as conversant as some of the rest of us with the conditions that existed in Saskatchewan during former depressions. I remember two or
102S
Unemployment Continuance Act

three other periods in which we had crop failures with consequent depression in that province. The Prime Minister mentioned the fact that no noise was made on this occasion. In 1914 there was a failure throughout the greater part of western Saskatchewan and relief was given, but no noise was made about it. Nor were the provinces and the municipalities bankrupt through the relief they extended. In 1919-20 it was necessary, in the part of the country from which I come, to give a good deal of relief, and again it was given without much noise. It was handed out through the municipality and handled very effectively. No noise was made about it.
We do feel that although the government have done a great deal in the way of affording relief, criticism is due for the very reason that the Prime Minister gave in his address on March 8, when he told us of the money that had been spent and the number of days' work that had been provided. But as my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) pointed out last night, it represented something over $10 for every day's work. The people are wondering why when such large sums of money were expended they received such meagre wages for the work they performed. Had the government adopted a reasonable policy we believe this situation could have been handled much easier. The high tariff legislation passed at the special session of 1930 has kept us out of the markets of the world and it has also kept up the prices of the products which the farmer is compelled to buy. During that session the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) gave the number of unemployed by provinces, and I quote from page 63 of Hansard as follows:
I find that at present in the province of Alberta there are 5,155 unemployed; during the winter it is contemplated that that number will reach 6,650. In British Columbia at the present time the unemployed number 7,692 and it is expected that during the winter that number will increase to 14,700. In the province of Saskatchewan the present number given is 5,276 and it is expected to rise during the winter to 8,201. In Manitoba the figure is now 6,950, with a possible 9,600 in the winter. In Ontario the figure is given as 49,367, rising to 82,214. In Quebec the present number is 41,190, as against an anticipated number of 49,290. In New Brunswick the present number is 500 and it is expected it may reach 2,850. In Nova Scotia the present number is 1,800 and it may rise to 2,350.
At that time there was a total of 117,930 unemployed and it was anticipated that by winter that number would increase to 175,855. As is recorded on page 64 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
If the measures which we submit to this house are productive of the good which we

anticipate, we hope that that number will steadily decrease, rather than increase.
As everyone knows, that number has not decreased. From the best information obtainable I believe that the number of unemployed to-day is three times the number given for September, 1930, and double the anticipated number for the following winter. This proves that the measures submitted at that time by the government have not been productive of the good anticipated and that the hopes of the Prime Minister have not been fulfilled with regard to what his legislation was going to do.
Why does not the government come to this house and say:	Our legislation has been a
failure. It should adopt the suggestion made the other day by my right hon. leader and try some other way of handling the unemployment question. It is quite evident to everyone that the measures adopted have been a failure and the very words of the Prime Minister admit that it has been a failure. We tried to make it clear, even as far back as September, 1930, that these measures in connection with the increase in tariff and abolishing the British preference could not be effective in relieving unemployment. The whole trouble with the government seems to be that it has a leader who is too autocratic in his manner. Why does he not admit that sometimes he may be mistaken? That is one of his defects; he will never admit that it is possible for him to make a mistake and he seems to have a following ready to believe likewise.
This government should face the facts with regard to trade conditions. It should realize what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) is reported in the newspapers as having said in Sarnia, to the effect that Canada's productive capacity is so far in excess of our needs as consumers that we must find a market abroad. Such a market can be obtained only by the exchange of goods with other countries. There is one fact which the government so far has not realized, and that is that the wheat crop of western Canada is the greatest single source of purchasing power there is in this country. That was the reason why we supported the Dunning budget of 1930; we realized that if Canada was going to continue to be fairly prosperous, as she had been for a number of years, it was necessary that something be done to assist the wheat growers of western Canada. Mr. Dunning stated something to that effect when making his budget speech. We believe to-day that had the Dunning budget been adopted we would have had a market in the old country for our

Unemployment Continuance Act
surplus products. We have not much wheat but we have many other products to sell. We believe that had that budget been adopted it would have gone a long way toward relieving unemployment and it would not have been necessary to spend the immense amounts of money which have been expended during the last year or two.
Hon. friends opposite are fond of referring to the fact that during the Liberal administration some 700,000 immigrants entered this country, and they give that as one of the causes of unemployment. I never was a strong advocate of immigration, but I say to the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) that he would find it interesting to compare the speeches he made three or four years ago with what he said only a few nights ago. We remember that a few years ago he said that Canada should be the Mecca for all the over-populated countries of the world, and I think he repeated that thought on more than one occasion. Now he is trying to condemn the former government for bringing in some 700,000 people in the last five years. He also referred to the fact that General McRae, who was then a member of the house, made on two occasions in 1928 and 1929, interesting addresses in this chamber regarding a great colonization scheme, and he said that that gentleman was then expressing only his own opinion, being a private member. I took the trouble to look up Hansard of 1928, and on page 21 I find that the present leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Bennett) in no uncertain language expressed his views on the question of immigration. This is what he said:
It is true that immigration is by all odds the most important question that can engage the attention of this house or of this parliament.
Further on he said:
It is high time that something be done to put the power of parliament unitedly behind an effort to bring people over and settle them in this country. We cannot continue as we are and maintain our present position very long. It is essentially important that we should induce more settlers to come to this country. I have pointed out this before, and I repeat it now.
Then as reported on page 22 of Hansard of the same year, the right hon. gentleman said:
Now, sir, this question transcends party; it is larger than the lives of parties because it strikes at the very life of this dominion. We must have settlers. We have in Canada facilities to take care of an additional population of from 15,000,000 to 17,000,000 people; we have
10,000,000 acres of untouched land within twenty miles of the railways; we have the
Peace River area and other portions of the country which are lying idle while the government is expressing pious hopes as to what will happen. I say the time has come when action must be taken.	_
It cannot be done in any small way; it cannot be accomplished in any niggardly way, but it must be done in a large way.
That is the leader of the Conservative party, the present Prime Minister speaking in 1928 as recorded in Hansard. What would have happened, I wonder, had the wishes of the right hon. gentleman been given effect at that time, and we had brought in not
15.000. 000, but even the tenth part of
15.000.	000? What would have happened if we had brought in 1,500,000 people when we have so many unemployed to-day? I am rather inclined very often to discount the words of the Prime Minister, and that is why I suggest taking just the tenth part of wihat he said and trying to realize what it would have meant.
As I have said, the policies that are adopted by the government have proved a failure in dealing with the question of unemployment. In conclusion, let me say this: that the so-called success of the government in dealing with the unemployment problem reminds me very forcibly of the man who said that for the last year he had eaten corn flakes every morning for breakfast and had taken corn syrup on his pancakes, but still his corns were no better than they were a year ago.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution that we are now discussing proposes to put into the hands of the government, that is of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), the power, without any reference to parliament, not only to spend all moneys necessary in the relief of unemployment and of farm distress, but also to take what steps he may deem requisite in respect of matters affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, and that at a time when we, the elected representatives of the people, are here willing to perform the duty which properly devolves upon us. As we on this side of the house understand the matter, the granting of such power would mean the surrender of all our rights and privileges, of all the duties and obligations which rest upon us as members of parliament. Indeed, it must be evident to hon. members opposite that such would be the case, and I believe the Prime Minister must also realize this.
If legislation is passed, based upon this resolution, we might just as well, as has been pointed out already, prorogue parliament. We shall have handed over to the Prime Minister complete power to deal with anything in any manner he sees fit, without any limitation,

Unemployment Continuance Act
whatever. My disposition in dealing with all matters involving constitution and procedure is to take a somewhat liberal attitude. I say that in the ordinary application of the term. While I am not unwilling to learn from the wisdom and experience of our forefathers, precedents are valuable to me only as they indicate a course that experience has shown to be sound. They ought not to be as chains to bind us, nor should they impose upon us obligations to follow a course that common sense would reject. Because judges have given certain decisions in the past and have based them upon certain principles, is no reason to my mind why judges down through all time should give similar judgments. The men who are willing to abolish old precedents and to establish new ones are, after all, the men upon whom we have to depend for everything in the way of progress in human affairs.
Having said that, having indicated my general attitude in regard to matters of constitution and precedent, I wish to say that when the Prime Minister a year ago brought down his bill, that it is now proposed to revive, I did not feel as strongly opposed to it as did the majority of the members on this side. I was prepared to recognize that the situation was somewhat unusual; that new conditions had arisen. I was ready to recognize that as regards the money feature of the bill, it would be difficult to give even an approximate estimate of the amount that would be required. Therefore, while entertaining very serious doubts as to the wisdom of granting such power, I felt that something might be said for the procedure advocated. I was not completely convinced by the arguments advanced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) when he dealt with the section of the bill relating to questions of peace, order and good government; yet I was willing to admit that perhaps there was some force to them. In that I may have been all wrong; perhaps I was, and I am willing to confess that in that respect I might have been. But -and I want to say that "but" with all the emphasis the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) attaches to it when he is arguing his case-the circumstances that confront us to-day are very different from those of a year ago, very different from what they were last session. Then we were just at the close of a. session of parliament; parliament was just about to prorogue, in all probability not to meet for six months. It might have been pleaded on behalf of the government at that time that they were facing new conditions; that an unusual situation had arisen; that they had no precedents to guide them and that we would simply have to 
trust them under the circumstances to do the best they could.
But that is not the situation to-day; parliament is in session. We have been in session only a short time, only five weeks, and there is every probability that we shall still be in session when the first of May arrives, the limit that is set for the continuance of this law that it is proposed to revive. A very different situation prevails to-day. We have had no opportunity to study thoroughly the report in regard to the operation of the act which has been tabled by the government. Under all these circumstances are we not justified in asking, why this legislation? It has already been pointed out that the Prime Minister has given no reason why he is asking for a continuance of these powers. The Prime Minister has asserted again and again that only by being granted these powers could he effectually deal with the many complex questions with which he was confronted. Indeed, he has admitted that there are very good reasons why these powers should not be granted. He says that he sympathizes with those on this side of the house in the arguments which they have advanced. He has admitted that their reasons have weight. Indeed his own words are:
I am reluctant in a constitutional sense to ask for a continuance of these powers.
No one realizes better than the Prime Minister himself that in asking for these powers he is doing violence to the constitution and departing from all established precedents, but he does not cast the constitutional question aside in the same free and easy manner as some of his supporters do. He knows that a serious question is here involved. He knows that he is making a serious demand upon this parliament when he asks for these powers. Under those circumstances is it not all the more incumbent on the Prime Minister that he should tell us why he is asking for these powers?
I have said, Mr. Speaker, that I am not a stickler when it comes to matters of precedent and the constitution. I do not like to be bound by the dead hand of the past, and I am willing to cast precedents aside if they interfere with our doing what we think is the right thing to be done. But when we are asked to do violence to the constitution of this country and to depart from the precedents which have been handed down to us and which the experience of the past has shown to be sound, surely we are not unreasonable when we ask the Prime Minister to tell us why we should make such a departure.

The confidence which the Prime Minister has in himself is amazing. Undoubtedly selfconfidence is a good quality in men, and it is a good thing for a man to have a high opinion of himself. Unless a man has some respect for himself and some self-confidence he is not going to get very far in this world, but after all, most of the vices which afflict men are simply their virtues carried to an extreme, and that would seem to be the case with the Prime Minister. As he is fond of scriptural allusions I might remind him of the saying that we should not think of ourselves more highly than we ought to think. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we may be forgiven if we have not that complete and perfect confidence in the Prime Minister which he has in himself and which evidently many of his followers share. Surely it is not consonant with the dignity of parliament that we should be asked to submit to the treatment that is now being meted out to us. Yet I suppose that the majority of the supporters of the government will fold their hands and quite tamely submit, and say:
Ours not to make reply,
Ours not to reason why,
Ours but to echo "aye,"-
when the Prime Minister speaks.
The Prime Minister further says, on page 993 of Hansard:
-and I will welcome any suggestion that others may offer towards the solution of the problem -I know of no way, except by this method, whereby we can assist the provinces and supplement the work they have to undertake.
I will welcome any suggestions, says the Prime Minister. What do those words mean? In the mouth of the Prime Minister they mean absolutely nothing. When he says that he will welcome any suggestions he is probably honest with himself, but he is so constituted that while he may think that he is welcoming the suggestions of others he is actually putting them completely aside, and acting according to his own free will. What about the suggestion which has been made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), a suggestion which I think I may safely say is concurred in by every member on this side of the house, and, if hon. gentlemen opposite would only speak their minds, is recognized, I believe, by them too as a reasonable suggestion.
No, no.

Well, let us see what is
the suggestion. It is that the government should bring down a supply bill appropriating the necessary amount to meet the exigencies
of the case, and that out of the money thus granted by parliament the government shall spend whatever is necessary to meet the needs as they arise between now and the first of May. * Coupled with that suggestion was the assurance by the leader of the opposition that such a supply bill would pass without any opposition from this side of the house. That was a reasonable suggestion surely. Why was it not accepted? That is the question I want to ask of the Prime Minister. Why is not that suggestion accepted? The Prime Minister has not told us. He has simply brushed the suggestion aside. What does he say? At page 991 of Hansard he says:
Now, so far as a supply bill is concerned,
I think it is fairly obvious to those who have followe'd me that to ask for any particular sum of money at this time in the form of a supply bill, with the usual limitations that are imposed upon such measures, would not meet the situation. In, our judgment at any rate, having regard to our experience, it would not.
He says it is perfectly obvious that a bill of this kind would not meet the situation. Well, I must confess that it is not perfectly obvious to me. That may be my fault. It may be because I am a little dull in the uptake, but I would ask the Prime Minister to have patience with those of us who are not trained in the legal profession, who perhaps have just ordinary minds that cannot grasp in a moment all the nice points involved in a discussion nor appreciate as quickly as does the Prime Minister the subtleties of an argument. I would ask him to have a little patience with us and try to explain to us why what is so perfectly obvious to him should not seem reasonable to us. He speaks of a supply bill with its usual limitations. Really it is amusing to hear the Prime Minister talk of limitations. When have we known the Prime Minister to recognize any limitations when he wanted to do anything? Yet, when it suits him, he pleads that the granting of money through a supply bill, because of limitations which attach to it-whatever they are-would prevent him affording relief to the distressed unemployed and the farmers he desires to help. In September, 1930, we passed a bill granting the Prime Minister $20,000,000. Under the terms of that act he was permitted to use the money in any way he saw fit up until the month of March, 1931. Well, why can he not do that now? If we could pass that bill at that time why cannot we pass a bill now to give him whatever money he needs until the first of May? The Prime Minister may say that there is a perfectly obvious difference between the two cases, but if there is any difference certainly it is all iu

favour of the suggestion made by the right hon. leader of the opposition.
It must be evident to hon. members that it is not the way in which the money is to be obtained which constitutes the reason the Prime Minister rejects this suggestion. There must be some other reason, and we can only conclude that it is because he desires to retain the power to amend Jaws, modify laws, abrogate old laws and institute new laws at his own sweet wilL A few evenings ago we listened to a very interesting and entertaining address from the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). When that rapid-firing gun gets into action we are always interested, whether or not he brings down any game.
I think he did.*

We always like to hear the Minister of Railways and Canals, although at times he makes us laugh-at least, we would laugh if the matter were not so serious. It was rather interesting to hear the Minister of Railways and Canals plead with hon. members on this side of the house to cooperate with the government. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to understand the meaning of the word "cooperation."
The hon. member understood it, all right.
Yes, and I am glad I did.

That was a long time ago.
. Mr. BROWN: I certainly did understand it, and it is because I understand the meaning of the term "cooperation" that I am trying to explain it to hon. gentlemen opposite. I am glad I am recognized by them as an authority on the subject, and for that reason I proceed with greater confidence. The Prime Minister does not want cooperation, as we understand it. He wants obedience, he wants submission, he want us to say "aye" when he says "aye" and to say "nay" when he says "nay." If all that happens the Prime Minister will be quite satisfied with the cooperation we give him, but he will be satisfied with nothing else.
What does cooperation mean? It simply means working together. How can we work together, how can any two persons work together unless each is ready at least to some
extent to compromise, to defer to the opinions of the other.
That is what we want you to do.

No, that is not what you want us to do, at all. You want us to do all the deferring, and you want to do none. You

want us to do all the compromising and sacrificing, yet you do not want to compromise or sacrifice. That is the kind of cooperation hon. gentlemen opposite want. There can be no cooperation on a basis of that kind. As I have said, cooperation means working together, and if we are to work together there must be a willingness to compromise and to defer to other opinions.
I want to ask if any hon. member has noticed any spirit of cooperation in the attitude of the Prime Minister. If he wishes to cooperate he must at least to some extent take us into his confidence, he must tell us about those emergent situations which he expects will arise, and to meet which he will need to exercise the arbitrary powers he asks. Perhaps he will say, "But I cannot do that in public." Well, he might at least do what Sir Robert Borden did at a critical period during the war when parliament was called to meet behind closed doors. If the situation is as bad as the Prime Minister indicates, that course might be taken.
You are away out.

People of Canada are beginning to ask whether we are being governed by a parliamentary system of government, or whether parliamentary government has become a fiction and we are now under an autocracy. Perhaps I am wrong when I say people are beginning to ask the question;
I think they have already satisfied themselves that this government has become an autocracy. History affords us examples of puppet kings. Evidently it is the desire of the Prime Minister to make this a puppet parliament-and,
I am sorry to say, at least in some measure he has accomplished his purpose.
During the remainder of the time at my disposal I purpose further to consider some matters I wished to bring before the house a few days ago when I requested the privilege of moving the adjournment of the house.
I wish to give an illustration of the manner in which some of these very urgent questions are dealt with by the present government. Of course, we do not expect the government to act with the speed indicated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) who said, in the city of Winnipeg, that within three days the Conservative party could set in motion machinery whereby unemployment would be cured. Although I am not using his exact words, I believe I am interpreting them correctly.
I shall have time to deal with only one case. Last August I, along with other hon. members, received a communication from the

Unemployment Continuance Act
director of unemployment relief at Ottawa asking us to give suggestions as to what work might be done. I made a tour of my constituency, coming into contact with the mayors, reeves or councillors of practically all the municipalities. In the course of that tour a certain situation was brought to my notice. It so happens that in a section of my constituency adjacent to the international boundary line there had been, in addition to drought, a very destructive hail storm. Consequently in that vicinity there was very little feed. Immediately across the border line from that point there are some hay marshes. Some of our own people had gone across the line to put up hay, of which a quantity was available at moderate prices. Those Canadians however were unable to bring in the hay because in response to demands of some of our friends from southern Alberta the duty on hay had been raised to $5 per ton. That was an impassable barrier between the hay and the starving live stock. So immediately I wrote to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) and on August 31 I got this reply:
Dear Sir,


Your letter of the 27th instant requesting free entry of hay for the use of farmers in your constituency has been received in Mr. Ryckman's absence in Europe.
As the minister will not return to Ottawa for some weeks, I have referred your request to the commissioner of customs for such action as the department may be able to take in the matter.
On September 2nd I received this letter from the private secretary to the minister: Dear Mr. Brown,

On my return from vacation and in the continued absence of the minister, who is in Europe, I find your letter of August 27th awaiting answer.
I note what you say as to the shortage of hay for feeding purposes in your district and the information which you supply with regard to the possibility- of securing some just across the international border.
In these matters, we act on the advice of the Department of Agriculture and I am, therefore, communicating to-day with the Hon. Robert Weir in this regard.
I thought at the time, perhaps foolishly, that the matter would be taken, in hand immediately by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and that in due course a satisfactory solution would be reached. However, as the months went by and nothing was done, on December 15 I wrote directly to the Minister of Agriculture. On December 31 I got this letter from him in reply:
I regret very much my delay in answering your letter of 15th December.
I put the subject matter of your letter before the Minister of National Revenue.
Passing the buck from one to the other.
Thanking you for bringing this to my attention.
But before I received this answer from the minister I got further word from the district affected that conditions were very serious, and consequently I wrote the following letter to the Prime Minister:
Dear Sir,-
I wish to call your attention to the very serious condition in regard to feed for live stock that prevails in one section of my constituency.
This district in question lies close to the international boundary and suffered very severely, both from hail and drought. The consequence is that there is not sufficient feed to see the stock through the winter. Indeed,
I am informed that in some cases the supply is already exhausted.
Now, it happens that just across the line in the state of Dakota there are some large hay marshes. Some of our people went over there and put up hay for themselves and there is besides a considerable quantity available at a reasonable price. The $5 a ton duty, however, interposes an impassable barrier between the hay and the starving live stock.
I wrote the Minister of National Revenue some months ago recommending that this hay be admitted free of duty. The reply I got was that in such matters they were governed by the advice of the Minister of Agriculture. I thought that the matter would be turned over at once to the Minister of Agriculture but, finding that that had not been done,-
I made a mistake there, because evidently it was turned over to the Minister of Agriculture.
[DOT]-I wrote the minister himself. Since writing him I have had further word that the situation is very serious and I am, therefore, giving you the information that I have already given two of your ministers.
There is no other feed available except what might be shipped in by railway and that would of necessity carry a high price.
Some of our people have wood that they would gladly exchange with their American neighbours for hay but they have no money to pay the duty.
I hope that this matter will receive your immediate attention and that you can see your way clear to have the customs officers at Snowflake and Windygates instructed to allow this hay in free of duty.

Your letter 23. Please write me Calgary names and quantity hay to be imported so that I may instruct action to be taken which can only be done by specific reference to transactions by individual importers. Seasons greetings and best wishes.

When I reached Ottawa I immediately called on the department interested and found that on the 4th of February an order in council had been passed-a general order not requiring the details the Prime Minister had asked from me. I will quote only a couple of paragraphs:
The undersigned, therefore, in order to mitigate the loss and damage above referred to, deems it right and conducive to the public good to recommend that authority be granted for the refund or remission of customs duty and taxes paid or ordinarily payable upon hay imported for feeding purposes into districts where the feed shortage referred to above exists and entered at customs between the 16th November. 1931, and the 30th April, 1932, both dates inclusive.
Here is the point to which I wish to direct the attention of the house:
A similar situation was dealt with by council in 1930, and order in council P.C. 55/253 of the 5th February of that year, authorized the refund or remission of customs duty payable upon straw imported for feeding purposes into districts where a shortage existed between 1st November, 1929, and the 30th April, 1930.

When I wrote the Prime Minister I had reason to know the facts of the case, because it was I who was responsible for having that original order passed. It was in connection with the same district as a matter of fact. I found such conditions prevailing there that I brought the matter immediately to the notice of the executive of the United Farmers of Manitoba, and they promptly got in touch with the Hon. Mr. Crerar, who. was then in Winnipeg. He was back in Ottawa in a few days, and a day or two later the order in council referred to was passed. It was all done inside two or three weeks. It took this government almost six months to accomplish the same results.
Was it done?

Yes, I must say I understand the result was satisfactory, but when cattle are starving time is the most important factor. I have had communication with the department, also with the officials in Winnipeg, but up to date I have had no satisfactory information as to exactly what took place in the correspondence between the two governments. I have called for the correspondence but it has not yet been brought down. I see it has been brought down in the Manitoba legislature, but so far we have had only newspaper reports and I have not had time to examine it. At present, therefore, we are in the dark. I do say that whatever the government does in the future it has been woefully negligent in the past in taking action at the opportune moment when, as I have said, time is one of the most important factors.
I shall not have time to go further into this question to-day. I may be able to do so on some future occasion, but reverting to the subject I was discussing in the first place, I would direct attention to the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor), who pointed out, in opposing this resolution, that we have been given no indication of the government's purpose. They ask us to grant them certain powers up to the first of May. But what after the first of May? Surely it is treating us without that consideration which is due to members of parliament who have been chosen by their constituents to represent them here. Our constituents may have been wrong in sending us here, but they have sent us and we wish to do the best we can to protect their interests. We wish to be treated with the dignity with which men who have been placed in this position should be treated. And it is not treating us with dignity when the Prime

They are thankful for what the government has done to relieve the unemployed, who, for the most part, are strangers attracted to this country by the intensive immigration policy of the former regime; and if we find Canadians among these unemployed, it is because foreigners have taken from them the means of earning their living.

After sitting
in this house listening to the debate of the last week, if it can be called a debate, I have come to the conclusion that the chief objection on the part of hon. members opposite seems to lie in the thought that the resolution now before the house is too stringently Conservative. Well, I am quite sure that those who are in need, even though they may think that this legislation is ultraConservative, feel that it is a happy and wholesome fault.
A few days ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in his speech said, as reported at page 705 of Hansard:
The women and children who are suffering in this country to-day have asked the Prime Minister for bread, they have asked him for work, but he has given them not even a stone. . . .
The same women and children are now asking for bread and the leader of the opposition has not given them even a speech. It seems to me that if all that this government has done for suffering humanity in this country can be called a stone, the people who have been given relief will very much prefer that stone to some of the idle chatter we have been forced to listen to in the last week. The people of Canada at this moment are wondering whether or not we are big enough Canadians to cast off this political leprosy that is threatening to destroy us in these times of danger and anxiety, and I suggest that if we are not big enough to do this we are not worthy to be called Canadians.
Some hon. gentlemen have said that what the government is looking for is suggestions. I would make one now, and it is constructive. I would suggest to hon. members opposite, who for the past week have been rehashing the speech made by the leader of the opposition last July, that they have it recorded on a series of gramophone records

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few
words in regard to the resolution before the house but before doing so I desire to speak, as a Saskatchewan member, in connection with the relief afforded to the distressed inhabitants of my province. I should like to say a few words in regard to the nature and extent of that relief, with regard to its administration and then with the permission of the house I am going to have the temerity to accept the invitation of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) and offer some suggestions as to future relief.
Primarily, I desire to register my objection to the renewal for two months of the powers conferred on the government by the statute which it is now sought to revive. I have been examining the report of the dominion director of unemployment relief and have studied the methods employed in granting relief in the province of Saskatchewan. I join with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) in saying that in my opinion the government has done its best to meet the difficulties which existed in that province. It has made mistakes-I think that has been admitted by hon. members opposite-but at the same time it has made a sincere effort to meet the difficulties. I note that the relief has taken some five or six forms. First, there was direct relief, and I notice that $4,275,991 was distributed before February 20, 1932, to give relief to approximately 53,727 families. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has stated that this amount has been considerably increased up to the present time and something like $5,250,000 has been distributed, which amount will suffice to aid the distressed people of southern Saskatchewan and other parts of the province at present in need.
Contributions have been made to the public works programs of cities, towns and villages. [Mr. B. M. Stitt.)
These works took the form of street improvements, the providing of water supply, the extension of existing water and sewage systems and other similar undertakings, which involved a large percentage of labour. Under this heading the dominion has expended something like $1,600,000.
An effort has been made to place men on farms, and in this connection the dominion expended $125,000. Single men experienced in farming were placed on the land over the winter. They received $5 per month and of course free board and lodging and the government granted a bonus to the employer farmer. This provided employment and at the same time it was a wise move to keep these men separated rather than to have them gather together in large numbers.
Contributions were made towards the cost of highways, and then there was the five-cent bonus on wheat. The people of Saskatchewan who were in distress are thankful to the people of Canada for the relief provided. They realize that this parliament voted practically an unlimited sum for the purpose of providing relief and I do not think they are unmindful of the fact that it was this government that conceived the legislation brought down in September last. However, having said that, I say now that with the knowledge gained during the past seven months no hon. member in this house should want to continue that type of relief. We have come to the conclusion that there are better ways of meeting the difficulty. I do not think we can blame the government for having taken the course it has, because it seemed the wisest thing to do, but I imagine that were it to set out to-day on a new course of relief it would find direct relief would be the cheapest, and that the payment to the farmers on an acreage basis would be more equitable.
I do not suppose the administration of relief is a federal matter and as far as I am concerned I can see no great reason to complain thereof. Many complaints have been made of the actions of some of the minor officials; there were some highly indefensible appointments made by over-zealous partisans, but taking into consideration the magnitude of the task and the enormous problem which confronted the government, the mistakes made were not more numerous than one might expect.
Having said so much, I come now to the resolution and here I find something to which I object. On its face this resolution is quite innocent; in effect the government says that in the year 1930 we gave it certain extraordinary powers, which it wants extended for an addi-

tional two months. This resolution does not sound very serious until it is examined. Many of the elected representatives of the people object to a renewal of these powers. Having once made a mistake, they do not wish to make it again. It has been frequently pointed out that section 2 contains the authority to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as the governor in council may in his discretion deem expedient to expend for three purposes, the relief of distress, the providing of employment and the maintaining within the competence of parliament of peace, order and good government throughout Canada. It is to this last provision that we object and must continue to object. I do not believe there would be a single speech from this side of the house if a bill were introduced to provide for the relief of distress and the supply of food and seed to the farmers. There would be no delay; we would cheerfully support such a bill but we fail to see either the wisdom or the necessity of renewing the powers to which I have referred; that of maintaining within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada. Why should it be necessary for the governor in council to take these powers to itself? Why should the government want to have these powers conferred upon it? Are not the general powers conferred by sections 87 to 98 of the criminal code sufficient for all purposes, sufficient to cover every possibility? Is it necessary to give relief with one hand and at the same time to exhibit the other, heavily mailed, to the person to whom the relief is being given? I do not think it is. If we examine the provisions of the criminal code, we shall find that all the power necessary for parliament to maintain peace, order and good government, is already conferred by some sections of the code.
