When the house rose I had just referred to the fact that the criminal code in my opinion contains within the borders of sections 87 to 98 inclusive sufficient safeguards against any unlawful behaviour that might be anticipated and which it was probably intended to anticipate in the words to which I have taken exception in the bill before the house. I wish now to point out that the sections to which I have referred give us the law concerning unlawful actions of individuals, unlawful assemblies and unlawful associations. I do not desire to weary the house, but I want to read one or two of the sections to which I have just referred. Section 87 reads as follows:
An unlawful assembly is an assembly of three or more persons who, with intent to carry out any common purpose, assemble in such a manner or so conduct themselves when assembled as to cause persons in the neighbourhood of such assembly to fear, on reasonable grounds, that the persons so assembled will disturb the peace tumultuously or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to disturb the peace tumultuously.
The following sections of the code up to and including section 97 contain within their four corners all kinds of penalties to discourage men from unlawful behaviour, the unlawful behaviour of the kind which is specified in the section which I have just read. I ,do not propose to read all these sections, but I should like to outline the provisions of each one.
Subsection two of section 87 which I have just read provides that an assembly lawfully assembled may become an unlawful assembly. That can be easily understood no doubt by every hon. member of this house. We can readily conceive of occasions when men might meet together with a lawful purpose in mind; perhaps one or two individuals among them might have an unlawful purpose in mind, and, by using inciting words, be the means of causing a hitherto lawful assembly to become inspired with unlawful motives and to do unlawful acts.
Section 88 defines a riot:
A riot is an unlawful assembly which has begun to disturb the peace tumultuously.
Section 89 prescribes the penalty for taking part in an unlawful assembly, the penalty being one year's imprisonment.
The next section prescribes the penalty for taking part in a riot-two years' imprisonment with hard labour.
Then in section 91, in order that the assembly unlawfully assembled and which may have developed into a riot may be dispersed, certain officials are charged with that duty- the sheriff, the deputy sheriff, the mayor or other head officer, and justice of the county, city or town affected, and later on I think that the word magistrate is used. They are

charged with the duty of reading a proclamation in the following terms:
Our sovereign lord the king charges and commands all persons being assembled immediately to disperse and peaceably to depart to their habitations or to their lawful business, upon the pain of being guilty of an offence on conviction of which they may be sentenced to imprisonment for life.
That is a severe penalty, one that should deter even the most hardened, unless their minds are absolutely set upon breaking the peace.
The next section, 92, provides imprisonment for life for persons who:
(a) with force and arms wilfully oppose, hinder or hurt any person who begins or is about to make the said proclamation, whereby such proclamation is not made; or,
fb) continue together to the number of twelve for thirty minutes after such proclamation has been made, or if they know that its making was hindered as aforesaid, within thirty minutes after such hindrance.
Section 93 provides for the arrest of persons who fail to obey the command to disperse within thirty minutes, and provides also that bystanders may be called to assist the officers that I have just enumerated. It goes further. It indemnifies those officers against any harm that may be occasioned those who resist them, even should the resistance lead to the death of the resister.	,
The next section provides one year's imprisonment for the bystander or other person who refuses to assist without reasonable cause and after reasonable notice the officer or officers who have proceeded to try to disperse the assembly.
The next section provides imprisonment for life for riotous destruction of property, and the next section, seven years' imprisonment for riotous damage to property.
Then we come to the much talked of section 98, which defines an unlawful association, and I shall read that subsection one of that section in full:
Any association, organization or corporation, whose professed purpose or one of whose professed purposes is to bring about any governmental, industrial or economic change within Canada by use of force, violence or physical injury to person or property, or by threats of such injury, or which teaches, advocates, advises or defends the use of force, violence, terrorism or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, in order to accomplish such change, or for any other purpose, or which shall by any means prosecute or pursue such purpose or professed purpose, or shall so teach, advocate, advise or defend, shall be an unlawful association.
I ask, could anything be more comprehensive?
I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but nothing concerning the criminal code is dealt with by the motion before the house.

What I was trying to
prove, Mr. Speaker, was that it was really unnecessary to include in the bill the words "for the peace, order and good government of Canada." I have been trying to demonstrate that the criminal code contains all the protection for the public and the crown that is necessary, and I hope that you will rule, sir, that I am in order and that it is permissible for me to proceed to prove that the provisions of the criminal code render unnecessary the provisions in this bill for a similar purpose. Am I in order?
Finally, as to the punishment:
Its officers-[DOT]
That is, the officers of an unlawful association :
[DOT]-may be arrested if they sell, speak, write or publish anything as the representatives or professed representatives of such association, or if they wear or carry about on the person any badge, insignia, emblem, banner, motto, pennant, card, button or other device whatsoever indicating membership or indirect connection with such association.
A sentence of twenty years is provided for that offence. Again I would ask, are not these provisions of the criminal code all comprehensive? Are not the penalties sufficient to meet any occasion that could possibly arise of the kind that it is sought to avoid? If not I think it is reasonable to ask what is it that the government anticipates that these provisions do not cover? It may be said that it was never in the mind of the government that this section was to deal with seditious utterances or unlawful assemblies. In that connection I might refer to the words of the right hon. the Prime Minister who, at page 4279 of Hansard of July 29, 1931, said:
In that regard the measure provides for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada. It is not for a moment to be thought that an insignificant number of strongly vocal persons shall be able so to affect the populace of this country as to make it impossible for us, in cooperation together as Canadians, to work out our destiny. I say that class happily, is few in number. But in this present situation they now see an opportunity propitious to the presecution of their pernicious political doctrines.
I find myself very much in accord with the Prime Minister in the sentiments he expressed therein. I contend however it is not necessary to revive an act containing the words:
. . . maintaining within the competence of parliament, peace, order and good government throughout Canada.

I have regarded him as an able and determined critic; sometimes I may have thought his language vitriolic. Now that I know him personally, however, I do not think that. I do say however that I have found no occasion upon which, when in opposition, he devoted any part whatsoever of his forty minutes to commendation of the government of the day.

My hon. friend's memory
is very short.
Possibly it is.
It is faulty.

However, I do not now
think he is so bad. Hansard is very expert in recording words, but it does not portray tones of voice or gestures, nor can it reproduce the pleasant smiles which often accompany my hon. friend's harsh words.
That is very fortunate.

Having said so much I
am sure the Minister of Railways and Canals will know I do not bear him any ill will because of his speeches made when in opposition. I have sometimes thought he must have been a close student of Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, because at page 415 of volume 2 I find the following:
The opposition exercise a wholesome influence upon parliamentary debate, and upon the conduct of the business of the crown in parliament, for they are the constitutional critics of all public affairs: and whatever course the government may pursue, they naturally endeavour to find some ground for attack. It is the function of an opposition to state the case against the administration: to say everything which may plausibly be said against every measure, act, or word of every member of the ministry:	in short to constitute a standing
censorship of the government, subjecting all its acts and measures to a close and jealous scrutiny.
I do not think the Minister of Railways and Canals is quite correct when he says there has been on the part of the opposition no commendation of government policies. On more
than one occasion during this session I have heard such commendations. Perhaps the commendations were guarded, the praise was faint, but even my hon. friend will agree that faint praise is better than utter condemnation.
I hope I am not doing the Prime Minister an injustice by assuming that when he inserted this particular clause in the bill he had it in mind that there might be some land of disorder in the country, disorders which I believe are covered by the provisions of the criminal code, to which I referred.
I notice, however, that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) held other views. Referring to the same passage in the bill, he is quoted at page 4439 of Hansard, July 31, 1931, as follows:
First and foremost, starting -with my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor), my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) and one or two others, have uttered the same criticism in regard to the appearance in this bill of the words, "peace, order and good government." There seems to be an idea that these words have been placed in this enactment for a sinster purpose. If the house wall reflect for a moment I think that it will realize that these words are the foundation of the authority of this parliament to pass such a measure. If the bill is not founded upon the theory that it is necessary to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada, then parliament would have no authority to pass it. Without these words the bill in tile form in which it is enacted into law might be set aside or challenged in the courts. The judgments of the privy council during recent years have established most clearly that unless there is something in the nature of a national disaster, of plague, famine, or some national emergency, then parliament has no authority to legislate upon the subjects set out in this bill.
I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to the two significant points in this comment of the Minister of Justice. First, he doubts whether parliament would have authority to pass such a measure as the one contemplated at that time, unless the words in question were inserted. Then he points out that if the bill were not founded upon the theory that it is necessary to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada, parliament would have no authority to pass it. I would not presume to question the validity of that argument. I do not know anything about the law, but I have an idea that even if the words to which we are referring were not inserted the parliament of Canada could pass a law granting assistance to the distressed and relief to the hungry and ill clad, and also could provide assistance for farmers.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like in the beginning to direct the attention of the house to a remark made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the other day in introducing this resolution. He referred to the fact that in the dried-out districts of Saskatchewan some 300,000 people are wholly dependent on relief for food, clothing and fuel for themselves and their families and feed for their stock during the present winter. He boasted, with some pardonable pride, that the Saskatchewan Relief Commission had looked after the needs of these people at a cost to the treasury iof five and a quarter million dollars. This sum divided among 300,000 people amounts to $17.50 apiece. That does not mean that a man in Saskatchewan can live all winter and feed his stock on $17.50. What it does mean is that in spite of the fact that those people have lost three successive crops, they have been able to come within $17.50 per capita of supporting themselves throughout the winter. I doubt if there is another class of people in Canada who if afflicted in the same way would have been able to show so good a record.

The 300,000 of course,
would cover families of farmers as well-men, women and children, which makes quite a difference.

He boasted the other night of the achievements of the Saskatchewan Relief Commission; he told us how efficient they were, how honourable and trustworthy, how impartially they had done their work. I agree with him. There is credit coming to that commission. From what I have seen they have functioned efficiently and impartially from the time they first began to function. No doubt if my hon. friend had so desired he could have set up a commission that would have played politics and would have tried to make political capital for himself and for his party out of the situation; but he did not do so, and we give him credit for it. I also want to commend his business sagacity for paying the money directly into the hands of the commission and not allowing it to pass through the hands of any intermediary. There again I think he is deserving of the commendation of the house.
But I want to ask him this question: If this Saskatchewan Relief Commission is so competent, so impartial, so trustworthy that it could be entrusted with the expenditure of millions of public money, why is not the commission sufficiently trustworthy to be permitted to set up its own organization; why was it not permitted to choose its own relief officers? Before that commission was set up a very efficient relief organization was in existence and was functioning in every rural municipality in Saskatchewan. It consisted of the reeve and councillors of the different municipalities. My right hon. friend on more than one occasion has stated in this house that relief is first the duty of the municipality, then of the provincial government, and then of the federal government. Now I say we had in each municipality an organization already functioning. Let me explain to those who do not know the situation in Saskatchewan that a municipality there is a block of country eighteen miles square divided into six equal parts called divisions. In each of 41761-66
those divisions resides a councillor elected by the people of the division and knowing every one of them and all their circumstances. The council is presided over by the reeve, also a resident of the municipality, and served by the municipal clerk, who knows everybody in the municipality and is fairly conversant with their affairs. That organization, I say, was functioning under the direction of the provincial government before the Saskatchewan Relief Commission was set up. It was an organization that would fit perfectly into the scheme^f the commission. All that was necessary when the commission was set up was to say to the municipal councils: In future you shall take your instructions from the commission and not from the provincial government. But the federal government did not see fit to do that. They decided to scrap that organization.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh no.
So far as administering relief is concerned, they did.
Would the hon. member say how he would propose to handle the administration of relief in the unorganized districts?

I am speaking of the
seventy-six municipalities referred to by my right hon. friend where the commission was handling one hundred per cent of the relief.

There are only two
small unorganized districts in the province.
There are large unorganized districts in the north, where many settlers from the dry districts have moved in and where a good deal of relief is being administered to-day.
There are some unorganized districts in the south, too.

In the month of August I received a long distance call asking me to attend a meeting in a remote corner of the Weyburn constituency. I went down on the appointed day and there met the reeve and councillors of the municipality and perhaps fifty ratepayers. They were very much concerned over the fact that nothing seemed to be doing in the way of getting relief in to them. It was nearly the end of the month of August, and I wondered what induced their fears. One man explained the situation, and as his case was typical of a good many others I will state it for the benefit of the house. He said: "I live thirteen miles from town. Before winter sets in it will be necessary for me to get out to my farm sufficient fuel and



Unemployment Continuance Act
supplies for the household and feed for the stock to carry me through the winter. In order to do that I shall have to travel with my team a total of 650 miles. If I can get at the work right away I can probably do it before the snow falls; if I cannot, if winter should set in before I get finished, perhaps I will not be able to get my supplies in at all." That was the situation which confronted those people, and caused their alarm. I had to do the best I could for my right hon. friend. I told them he was a man of wonderful energy, great driving force and marvellous capacity for getting things done, that we had given him all the money of Canada and all the power of parliament, and I had no doubt whatever if they had a little patience he would soon have relief sent into them in abundance. But that did not quite satisfy them, and I consented to go into Regina next day and find out when they could expect action. I went to the offices of the Saskatchewan Relief Commission. The first question I asked was when they expected to get under way, and the reply was, as soon as they got their organization completed. My next question was: What kind of organization are you setting up? They said, "We are going to have in each rural municipality a relief officer who will draw a salary of $75 per month plus an allowance for the use of his car"-not an excessive salary considering the work he has to do.
Would you mind telling us whom you saw?
One of the commissioners.
Which one?
The chairman.
Mr. Black?

Yes. He said the relief officer would be assisted by a committee of five local persons, four men and one woman, who would work without salary. The first duty of the relief officer, I was told, would be to visit every home in the municipality with forms which he would fill out in the presence of the applicants. It is quite an extensive form, on one page of which there is a statement of the man's assets and liabilities, and there are numerous questions as to his needs and how far he can supply them himself for the winter. The relief officer was to go in person to every house and fill out the form. That done, he would call the committee together and go over the applications with them and they would decide how much relief each person was entitled to.
I tried to explain to the commission that if the relief officers got out the very next week,

which would be the first of September, it would be the latter end of October before they could get the information, and that if winter should set in before that a good many people would be caught in a very sorry plight. I asked, "When will your relief officers start out?" The reply was, "They are not appointed yet." I made inquiries from other sources then to find out how the relief officers were to be appointed, and this is what I discovered: that a Conservative organizer from another part of the province had been sent by the Saskatchewan government-
What was the source of that information?
Give us the facts.

Tell us the source of
the information.

If what I state is not in accordance with the facts, hon. gentlemen will have a chance to deny it. A Conservative organizer from another part of the province walked into the office of the Saskatchewan Relief Commission and said, "I will select your relief officers for you."
If the hon. gentleman will permit me, I do not know where he got his information, but I do say that the statement is not true.
Order.

This gentleman went out
through these seventy-six rural municipalities and selected seventy-six relief officers.
He didn't.

Another statement
that's not correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman is not making that as a statement of fact. He may have been so informed-
He dreamed it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -but it is not so.

The wish was father to
the thought.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was there after.

I was there too. I will tell
you something else. Two weeks later I was back in the office of the commission again because no action was visible. I asked what the delay was and this was the answer I received: "We are going to appoint relief officers at the next meeting of the commission; we have the list before us now," and the

Unemployment Continuance Act
gentleman who submitted the list was there that day. Now, these relief officers appointed by this gentleman, so far as I have seen them, have been good and efficient men. I have no fault to find with them.
What are you talking about then?

This is what I am pointing out. While this new organization was being set up, the old organization having been discarded, nothing was being done. Weeks and weeks of valuable time were lost. The people in those districts were out of coal; they had no feed for their stock, and they could not get it because the commission was not yet functioning. All this delay-why?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What time was that?
The second time I was there in the office.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But what day of the
month, do you remember?

The second time I was in
the office was September 8. On that date they told me they would appoint their officers the following Saturday, and after these appointments were made all the work I have outlined as having to be done by the relief officers had to be carried out. The result was that it was months and months before some people got their first relief order. I know people in my neighbourhood who did not get their first relief orders until December.

I know some that
didn't apply until February.

Well, I know some that applied as soon as their applications were taken and they did not get their first order until December. I do not criticize the commission nor the relief officers; what I am complaining of is the fact that the old organization was scrapped before the new one was ready to function. Now, if winter had set in early, if we had had a normal winter season, setting in in October-
Why not September?

Well, the year before winter set in the middle of October. I say, if winter had set in about the middle of October and we had had a normal amount of snow it would have been impossible for many people to get in their supplies. The commission has functioned and functioned well; but, I repeat, if we had had a normal amount of snow last winter the organization would have broken down completely.
41701-66i

Aren't you sorry there
wasn't a lot of snow?
No, I am not.
What is all the mourning about?
Give the man a chance; he has kept quiet all day.

The relief officer in the municipality in which I live has to unload feed at no fewer than eleven railway points and he must be present at every point. His assistants can give out the feed but he has to be there.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. Does the relief officer have to be present for every icar of feed unloaded, or has he made arrangements whereby the .elevator man or some other person may unload in his absence?
He doesn't know.

Some other man can unload provided the relief officer has made arrangements for the release of the car; but he has to go to the station and arrange with the agent to release the car. The point I am emphasizing is that if we had had even a normal amount of snow this winter it would have been impossible for the relief officer to get from one station to another to attend to that work, and the organization would have broken down; whereas under the old organization, with the councillor in each division, there was always someone on the ground to look after these matters. We were saved from a calamity last winter, not by the foresight of hon. gentlemen opposite but by reason of the fact that we had summer weather practically up to Christmas. We were saved by the "grace of God" as the Prime Minister would say.
And not by chapter 58.

Exactly. Again, I ask, if the Saskatchewan Relief Commission is so trustworthy that they can be entrusted with the task of looking after all these affairs, why were they not allowed to buy the hay sold to the settlers? They bought grain and it came in at a reasonable price; and they arranged for food, clothing and other commodities. But the hay was purchased by the Saskatchewan government and sold by the commission.

They were buying hay all through the fall. That was why it was purchased by the government.

A good many contracts were let for hay before the commission was set up. The municipalities had made an estimate of what hay was required in all municipalities, and this they submitted to the government. When the commission was set up the government notified the municipalities not to send in more orders for hay and the municipalities stopped. Hay was not coming in and I went to inquire why. The commission said they were not handling it. Then I went to the government. They said they supposed they would be handling it. I said: "The muni. cipalities do not know that you are going to handle it; you say you will handle it if they send you their orders, but they have been advised by the Minister of Municipal Affairs not to send any more orders. Will you advise them right away to send in their orders?" He said, "I will." A week later I went to a municipal clerk and said, "What about it; have you received any such instruc-. tions?" He said: "The instructions we have received are that we are not to order any more hay." It was delay and uncertainty from one end to the other, and it was months before many -people got any feed. The farmers in my own neighbourhood were dividing with each other their last bales of hay. They were forced to do this because none was coming in. Why was the relief commission not permitted to buy hay when they were selling it? We know that hay was the dearest thing that was sent in to the district, the one thing that was not bought by the commission.
Reference was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to the notes being taken from the farmers. I do not question for a moment the -truth of his statement that some of them insisted that they would not accept relief unless they were permitted to pay for it, but it does not follow that they had to be compelled to sign notes. The man who insists on paying an account is not generally required to sign a note. Any farmers I have met are really concerned about these notes. They tell me that they have never signed notes before without having to pay them, and they believe that pay day will come. When this matter was under discussion the Prime Minister stated that since he came into power hundreds -of notes taken from farmers many years ago for relief had come before the council for review and adjustments had been made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The adjustments were
made imder a statute passed a few sessions ago, and the council merely confirmed those adjustments.

Whatever the arrangement
may be, I suppose the inference is that later there may be some adjustment of these notes. I doubt whether that is a wise plan. I wonder w-ha-t effect it will have, say, on the political morals of the people. Suppose a government -it might be this government, it might be another-has in its possession past due notes signed by ninety per cent of the people in a given territory. When election time comes round the candidate of one party will say: An adjustment is to be made; if you vote for me probably I can get you a better adjustment than the -other fellow. The candidate of the other party will say: He cannot get you an adjustment; his party is going to be defeated; you had better vote for me. The issue in -that particular constituency would be: Who is going to give the best adjustment? I do not say that that is the intention of the Prime Minister, but that will be the result if these notes are held over the heads of the farmers with the promise of an adjustment later. I think it would be fairer and more in the interests of everyone if the Prime Minister would accept the suggestion made some time ago that the farmers in these districts be given a credit on their notes equal to one dollar per acre on the acreage seeded last year. This would act as a sort of equalizer between them and the farmers in the northern part of the province who received five cents per bushel bonus on their wheat.
I wonder if the Prime Minister ever stops to consider just how his conduct in regard to unemployment relief looks to hon. members on this side or to the people in the country generally. Let me review the attitude he has taken towards this house ever since he has been in power. He called parliament together in September, 1930, for the express purpose of relieving unemployment. He introduced a bill authorizing him to spend $20,000,000 to relieve unemployment, and side by side with that -bill he brought in a tariff bill which could have no other possible effect than to increase unemployment. Then he told us that unless we put these measures through quickly he would not go to the Imperial conference. We held our peace and let him go to the conference. The next year when parliament assembled, as was to be expected and as we predicted, unemployment was worse than ever. Parliament assembled in March and I do not think there was a single week in that session when someone on this side did not get up and ask the government what it intended to do in the matter of unemployment and farm relief. No answer was given

Unemployment Continuance Act
until well on in the summer, when one day the Prime Minister told us he would bring in a bill as soon as the order paper was cleared. In other words, there would be no relief granted until we stopped talking. He brought in his bill at the very end of the session when the order paper was cleared. Again we passed the bill under protest, and when the session was over he went out into the country to reply to the criticisms which had been levelled at him for the delay. He said it was our fault because we had talked so much, and that was why he could not bring in the bill.
That sounds reasonable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: History repeats itself.

The present session was
called early in February because my right hon. friend had agreed with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to call parliament before the relief act expired in order that we might consider what further action should be taken. Parliament assembled on February 4, but not a word was said about unemployment relief. On February 16 I rose in my place and asked the Prime Minister if it was the intention of the government to bring in another measure before the old act expired, and he replied that they were considering the matter. They continued to consider it until the other measure was as dead as a doornail.

Why doesn't the
hon. gentleman be accurate?
No effort was made to bring this matter before the house until after the act was dead.

Again you talked
too much.

We refrained purposely
from debating the address because we wanted to give the right hon. gentleman a chance to introduce his legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was not the reason.

Now the right hon. gentleman asks for an extension! to May 1 of the powers granted under the old act. What will happen on May 1? I have not the slightest doubt that when that date comes around the Prime Minister will come before this house with another measure equally obnoxious and he will say: There is unemployment and distress in the country, but the people will have to wait for jobs and for relief until you pass this measure and give us authority to do the thing we want to do.
And there will be another imperial conference.

I have no doubt that he will once more put the gun to our heads and say:	Unless you submit to this again, the
people will have to wait for relief. I wonder how long the unemployed of this country are going to submit to being used as hostages by the government to force the opposition into submission? What does the Prime Minister want anyway? He is asking us to clothe him with the absolute powers of a dictator. There are times when men will submit to a dictator, but the first essential of a dictator is that he be able to carry to a successful conclusion the thing he undertakes to do. What has the Prime Minister undertaken to do since he came into office? He undertook to build up Canadian industry by means of his protective tariff, and early in the session he told us that during the past year one hundred new factories had been established in Canada because of his tariff policy. He did not tell us that during the same period 464 factories had closed their doors.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No one else could tell
the hon. gentleman that.
The Bureau of Statistics can.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

Yes. He undertook to relieve unemployment. According to his own figures there were 200,000 unemployed when he came into office; to-day there are approximately
500,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is absurd.
Absurd?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Let us look at manufacturing, the industry which my right hon. friend has taken under his own special care. Let us see what has happened in this branch of industry. In September, 1930, 7,334 factories reporting to the Bureau of Statistics showed a pay-roll of 1,023,633 persons. In February of this year, after eighteen months of imy right hon. friend's policy, the reports from 7,766 factories-more than for the previous period -showed a pay-roll of only 819,174 persons. There was a decline of 204,458 in the number of those employed in the industry which my right hon. friend undertook to build up. When he says that there were not 500,000 unemployed in Canada, I say that in manufactur-

Unemployment Continuance Act
ing alone 204,000 persons have been thrown out of employment, and everybody knows there are large numbers in other lines of industry also out of employment. So that the figure of 500,000 cannot be far wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend wants to be fair. That is the season of greatest unemployment. If my hon. friend will follow the index figures, he will find that the diminution of employment in February of this year was less than it has been heretofore, and this is amazing, having regard to the situation in other parts of the world.

February is not the season of activity in outside occupations, but it is the month when most of our factories are giving employment, when they are getting ready for spring work, so that the falling off of 204,000 in the number employed in our factories is condemnatory evidence.
My right hon. friend undertook to open new markets; in fact I think he said he would blast his way into new markets for us. The first market he was to open was that of New Zealand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, that was open before we took office.
Then my hon. friend used the wrong word. He meant to say: I shall close markets.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The notice terminating the treaty was given before we came into office.

We know what action was taken at the short session when the Prime Minister of New Zealand was here, in this very chamber. We know what its effect was on the parliament of that country when he returned home, and we know the effect produced on trade between the two countries. We know what the right hon. gentleman did when he went to the Imperial conference, and we know what the effect was on imperial trade.
The Prime Minister aJlso undertook to Shut out butter, eggs, fruits, beef, mutton and innumerable articles that were coming into this country, and he is now boasting that he shut them out. The reason they are not coming into Canada is that the present price is so low that people in other countries cannot afford to sell them in Canada. If he wants to take credit for shutting those goods out of this country, he must also assume full responsibility for the decrease in their prices.
Is it not true that at the present time the price of butter in Canada is between four and five cents a pound higher than it is in the United States?
My right hon. friend was going to shut out butter so that we could have in Canada a market of our own higher than the world market.
That is not an answer to my question.
He was going to give the farmer a better price for his butter. All I have to do when speaking to the farmers is to ask them: Are you getting a better price for your butter?
Answer the question: yes or no.
The hon. member was elected on butter.

My right hon. friend also undertook to reduce the imports of manufactured goods. He boasts that he has done that also, but in doing that he has reduced the exports and the only thing he has to boast about now is that we are doing less business than we were before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that Canada has risen from sixth to fifth place amongst the exporting countries of the world?
We were that long ago.

My right hon. friend may find some consolation in the fact that other countries are hard up too, but that does not help to feed our hungry people or to put money into the packets of the farmers. He promised us prosperity in Canada, and it is no argument now to say that conditions are no worse than in other countries. Therefore I must say, from whatever point of view we contemplate the right hon. gentleman's policy, it has been a failure. He has faded to carry his undertakings to a successful conclusion no matter what he has undertaken. Why, then, should we make him a dictator? The first essential of a dictator is that he should be able to do successfully the thing he sets out to do. He is not therefore, the stamp of man for a dictator. The only reason he can assign why we should make him a dictator is that he has the will to dictate.
We cannot support -this measure, because the right hon. gentleman is asking for arbitrary powers. He is asking for powers which will make him practically a czar, or, as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) would say, a sultan. We made him an offer to pass any supply bill he would bring in, to vote him any amount of money he deemed necessary for the

Unemployment Continuance Act
purpose. He saw fit to reject this offer simply because he wants us to vote him dictatorial powers and unlimited control over the lives and property of our citizens. We refuse to give our consent to any such course.

Mi.
Speaker, let me add a word to what has already been said on this resolution which is supposed to resurrect the defunct act for the relief of unemployment and distress. I shall not try to demonstrate the unconstitutionality of this measure, because this has already been dealt with very ably by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) and others who have spoken.
I cannot support this resolution. Even had it been presented before the expiry of the original act, I should have questioned the advisability of continuing that measure, because I sincerely believe it has failed to relieve unemployment. Later on I shall give the reasons why I cannot support it.
Let me say first that during the election of 1930 the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and all his supporters made of the unemployment situation a national question. In a speech which the Prime Minister made in Montreal on June 26, 1930, and which is reported in the Montreal Gazette of June 27, he said:
Unemployment has become a national problem in Canada. It is the direct result of nine years of unsound economic policies applied by the Liberals.
My hon. friends opposite came into power with the motto that the crisis was due to Liberal administration. They said that the machine for the relief of unemployment would be at work three days after the election and that the people of Canada by the thousands would enjoy employment. At the first session we expected a great deal of practical work along that line, but the first thing the government did at the short session was what? Was it not for the relief of unemployment? The first thing they did was to abolish the tariff commission. Then there was a wholesale increase in tariffs. That was supposed to be the great panacea to cure all ills, not only for the present but for the years to come. They started to apply those tariffs in a wholesale way, and the direct result, as soon as they were applied, was that protests arose from ocean to ocean, and the next day they had to undo a great part of what they had done. It was a case of taking one step forward and two steps backward. They applied prohibitory tariffs all around, and soon their effects became apparent. Industry became stagnant, farming moribund, merchants bankrupt, the professional men financially embarrassed, and the labouring men were in misery and distress. Conditions have gone from bad to worse. AfteT applying this great panacea, in the last moments of the short session parliament voted an appropriation of twenty million dollars to the government for the relief of unemployment. The sum of twenty million dollars looks very nice to the public eye, but when we stop and consider what it really means to a country with ten millions of people, and when we consider what this twenty million dollars actually did in the way of public works and undertakings, it was very little indeed. I believe that if the money had been spent in a conscientious way, some benefit would have resulted from its expenditure, but very little benefit has been felt.
What was done with that twenty million dollars? Examples have already been given to the house in the last few days by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot), the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr.Heenan) and the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). In answer to them we have heard from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), who replied particularly to the exMinister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). I have been told that the Minister of Labour is a good politician. He is certainly pretty good when it comes to playing with figures, but I shall have to listen to him for a while yet before he will have proved to my satisfaction that he is a great statesman. He gave a whole lot of figures, and then to show that the work which had been done had met with approval he secured a lot of letters from mayors of different municipalities denying that political influence had been used in the distribution of the money. These letters came from municipalities where he is well known, and naturally these municipalities and mayors did not dare say anything to the contrary. They are eating out of the government's hand, and if they dared say anything different they would not get anything. The minister concluded his speech in a pompous manner, lauding himself and the government a la Ferguson.
I want to show you now, Mr. Speaker, how the money was unjustly distributed. Let me give an example of what happened in one part of my district on the road construction from Mattawa to North Bay. At first the people around there were told during the short session that inside of a month or two everyone who wanted work would have plenty of work. Then later they were told that the work would be started in two or three months,

Unemployment Continuance Act
and then they were told that it would not be started until the spring of 1931. But no work had started in the spring of 1931, and the months continued to elapse until September or October before the work was actually started. Here is what happened. The engineers worked for over a year laying out the survey of the road from Mattawa to North Bay, a distance of fifty miles. After the work was started, it was soon curtailed in many places and in other places stopped. No wonder the work was soon stopped. At the head of the work was a road commissioner who was paid $2,400 a year. There was an engineer paid full time, with two assistant engineers also paid full time; a chief of police and two assistants paid full time. Then there was a game warden, although I might tell you gentlemen that the territory between Mattawa and North Bay has been open to civilization for fifty years, and if all the people at work were to hunt the whole day long they could not find a chipmunk. In addition there was a publicity man on full time, sending articles to the newspapers of the country which the Nugget of North Bay and the Sudbury Star would have been glad to do for nothing. Then there was a photographer obtaining pictures of the men at work. All that ran away with a whole lot of money. There was also a doctor engaged on full time, when all along that line there are doctors working day in and day out for nothing for the poor people who cannot pay. Why were they not given a chance to make a few dollars on this work? But no, the government employed an outsider, a friend of the government, I suppose. After all this overhead expense and the employment of all these full-time officials, it is no wonder that the works were curtailed in many places almost as soon as they had started, and in other places were stopped entirely.
The Minister of Labour stated in the house the other day that $70,000,000 had been spent, of which $17,000,000 had been paid by the federal treasury, and that 334,300 people had been employed for a total of 7,415,000 days' work That means $70,000,000 for seven million days' work. That means that the government spent ten dollars a day. I would ask hon. members to remember that figure. Let us be generous and suppose that the labourers on this work got three dollars a day. Where did the other seven dollars a day go? In overhead expenses. It is no wonder that the work was curtailed and in many places stoppe'd soon after it was started.
Instead of relieving unemployment, unemployment has been on the increase ever since

this government came into power, and I have proofs of that statement right in my own district. The unemployment situation is so acute and the people have become so discouraged that some time ago I received a letter from a man asking me if it was true that there was some organization that would buy the corpses of cripples for dissection for experiments. He wanted to mortgage his body before death. That shows to what circumstances he must have been reduced. Although the government professes to see signs of improvement all over the country, the municipalities which cooperated with the government have gone the limit. They went to the very verge of bankruptcy, and some actually went into bankruptcy. Other municipalities were wise enough to stop before they actually went into bankruptcy. In my own city they have thought it wiser to give direct relief rather than unemployment relief work. I quote, from the Sudbury Star of February 24, 1932, the report of the relief inspector:
At the end of last week there were 4,100 persons receiving relief.
I ask hon. members to bear in mind however that the population of Sudbury is only about 20,000, and that the number receiving relief constitutes about one-fifth of the total population. The article continues:
According to the record of the relief inspector, Frank Rothery, of these 898 were heads of families, 2,187 are dependents and 15 are singles, such as widows and aged people. This does not include the men who are getting free meals at the soup kitchen.
This article would indicate that there was so much overhead expense in connection with relief work measures that very little actual relief was given, and unemployment has been continually on the increase.
What did hon. members and the country expect at this session? Everybody expected a.n extensive program for the relief of unemployment. About that however we did not see one word in the speech from the throne, and the Canadian people are still waiting for a constructive program. In the judgment of the public the ministers of the government are playing politics. They are busier finding fault with others than taking care of the country's business. The people are not in the mood to listen to political speeches such as those made by some of the ministers. Unemployment is on the increase. In many cases properties are being confiscated both in the country and in the cities.

To sum up the results, and not to mince matters, the experiment has proven a success.
Then on page 41 of Sir Rider Haggard's report we read:

The value of the security is increasing yearly as shown by the annexed documents of valuation. If a settler dies or moves away the value of his equity is more than enough to pay his obligations to .the Salvation Army and others.
Some of these people on one of the colonies gathered together and passed a resolution of which the following is a short extract:
We would like the benefits which we, our wives and families are receiving to be extended to the thousands who have been longing and praying for such a chance.
Then, at page 77 Colonel Holland remarks:
As I have pointed out prosperity has been much retarded owing to the causes given, but our people are self supporting. They are making some payments and improving their buildings. They are certainly in a much more flourishing condition than they ever would have been had they remained in the city.
Someone will say, "Why talk about a scheme like that? We cannot afford to do anything of the kind." May I point out that the other day the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) outlined a scheme by which a plan such as I have described could be financed. As regards these particular people there is no doubt that some government in Canada must pay for their keep. Three, four or five hundred dollars a year must be advanced to keep them from starvation. If a small amount of money were advanced by way of credit, and the people benefiting thereby were carefully chosen, having special regard to their record and their ability, experience and military service, and if the lands were properly selected, it seems clear that many who are unemployed and now have no hope for the future would be given fresh courage, and their conditions vastly improved. It may be suggested that such an arrangement would add to the overproduction of farm products. If that were the case we might conclude that we had succeeded far beyond our hopes, because we would expect that they would produce no more than sufficient food for their own use. No great or vast scheme need be undertaken. Individuals might be located in suitable places, and arrangements could be made to have groups who could work together located in the same district.
This is not a scheme to take people from one country and plant them in a far distant land where conditions are new and strange. They would be right within the borders of our own country, and would be familiar with the conditions. In the city whence I come there is a group of thirty men every one of whom has seen service in the trenches and has had farming experience. They are willing and anxious to have an opportunity to go to some

district where they could farm, but they would need government help. Anyone who is familiar with farm work knows that there is always work to be done about a farm. No one except the man who from day to day and from week to week has experienced unemployment can realize the sense of disappointment it produces and its demoralizing effect upon body, mind and soul. Officers now attached to the department might undertake this work. They would need the assistance of voluntary organizations throughout the country and could choose, from the ranks of the unemployed, men who would be suitable for work on the land. In that way I believe the number of unemployed would be reduced and as a result there would grow up in Canada a self-reliant and self-supporting group of men who would add much to the prosperity of Canada, and relieve the treasury of calls for charity.

My hon. friends opposite disclaim any politics in the matter, but they do not believe what they say. Where, under this act, do they get authority to take promissory notes, seed grain liens, except by some deceptive use, undreamed of a year ago, of this measure?
The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.
